# VRFSceneTemplateAsset

**Class** · namespace `VRFramework.Core.Editors.SceneBuilding` · assembly `VRFramework.Core.Editors` · [view source](https://git.cie-group.cz/vr-framework/vrf4/core/-/blob/interaction/physics-hold/Editor/SceneBuilder/Scene/VRFSceneTemplateAsset.cs#L27)

A scene template authored in the project rather than in code: which installers to run and
which prefabs to drop. This is what makes templates lasting rather than one-off - capture a
scene you are happy with, keep the asset, apply it to the next scene and the one after that,
and hand it to whoever builds the next module - and it lets a project offer its own
templates without writing an editor script.
Create one from Assets > Create > VR Framework > Scene Builder > Scene Template, or from the
"Save Scene as Template" card in the Scene Builder.
The VRF prefix is load bearing, not decoration. Unity has its own
UnityEditor.SceneTemplate.SceneTemplateAsset, and an "t:Type" asset search matches on the
short type name with the namespace ignored - so while this was called SceneTemplateAsset,
Unity's own scene-save hook picked our assets up as if they were its own, failed to load
them as its type and threw a NullReferenceException on every scene save. Do not rename this
back.

```csharp

public class VRFSceneTemplateAsset : ScriptableObject
```

## Methods

### CaptureActiveScene() {#captureactivescene}

Captures the open scene: a copy of the scene itself, saved beside the template, plus the
list of framework installers the scene satisfies so a later apply can top up anything the
copy is missing. Returns the created asset, or null when the user cancelled.
The scene is written with saveAsCopy, so the editor stays in the scene the user is
working on and their own file is neither switched nor marked saved.
